mainTopic: דיחוי in קדשים, unresolved questions about betrothing in halves or with one פרוטה for several things, and the dispute over appraising silk used for קידושין
overview: The amud opens by finishing a discussion about קדשים. From an animal that was made holy one half at a time, the גמרא learns three rules of דיחוי: it applies to live animals, to something unfit from the very start, and to holiness of monetary value. Then רבא asks a chain of questions about betrothing a woman "half by half." Does a man who betroths each half separately split the קידושין into pieces that cannot work, or is he just counting toward one whole betrothal? רבא, רב פפא and רב אשי then ask how a single פרוטה works when it is meant for more than one thing: two daughters for two sons, a daughter and a cow, or a daughter and land. Every one of these questions ends in תיקו. Next comes a real case of a man who made קידושין with silk garments, and רבה and רב יוסף argue whether the silk must be appraised first. The גמרא narrows the argument to the case where he said "fifty" and it really is worth fifty. A second version says they argue even when he said "any amount," and רב יוסף's reason, that שוה כסף must be like כסף, continues on the next amud.

steps.title: Three lessons about permanent rejection of offerings
steps.stepSummary: From the ruling just before this (an animal consecrated half at a time is holy but cannot be offered), the גמרא learns three general rules about דיחוי.
steps.simpleTranslation: Learn from this: living animals can be permanently rejected. Learn from this: something rejected from the very start counts as rejected. And learn from this: rejection applies even to holiness of monetary value.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is pulling three general rules out of the case it just discussed. In that case, an animal was made holy in two halves and can never be brought as a קרבן.
steps.deeperAnalysis: First, the animal is still alive, yet it is permanently pushed off the מזבח, so דיחוי works on live animals too. Second, the animal was never fit to be offered even for a moment, and it is still considered pushed off, so דחוי מעיקרא counts as real דיחוי. Third, the first half had only money-holiness (קדושת דמים), and דיחוי still applies.

keyTerms.meaning: Learn from it: we can draw this rule from the case
Living animals can be permanently rejected
Rejected from the very start, never fit even for a moment
Rejection that applies to holiness of monetary value

steps.whatToRemember: One case gives three rules of דיחוי: it works on live animals, it works from the very start, and it works on money-holiness.
steps.whyThisMatters: These three rules are built-in assumptions about דיחוי. They come up again wherever קדשים are disqualified.

phrases.english: Learn from this: living animals can be permanently rejected,
phrases.notes: "This" is the ruling right before here, about an animal that was made holy one half at a time.

phrases.aramaic: וּשְׁמַע מִינַּהּ דָּחוּי מֵעִיקָּרָא הָוֵי דָּחוּי,
phrases.english: and learn from this: something rejected from the start counts as rejected,
and learn from this: there is rejection even with monetary holiness.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Closes the previous discussion by drawing general rules from the ruling about the half-consecrated animal.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: דיחוי applies to live animals, to something unfit from the start, and to קדושת דמים.

steps.title: Betrothing each half of a woman with half a coin
steps.stepSummary: רבא asks about a man who says "half of you with half a פרוטה, and half of you with half a פרוטה." Did he split the betrothal into two parts that cannot work, or was he just counting toward one full פרוטה?
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא asked: if he says "Half of you with half a פרוטה, and half of you with half a פרוטה," what is the law? Since he said "half a פרוטה," did he cut his statement into separate parts? Or maybe he was just counting along toward the total?
steps.whatsHappening: A new topic starts here. רבא asks whether this two-step way of betrothing works.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Half a פרוטה is less than the smallest value that can make קידושין. If each half is a separate act, neither half works, so the betrothal fails. If he is only "counting along" (מונה והולך), the two halves add up to one full פרוטה for the whole woman, and it works.

keyTerms.meaning: He raised a question that could go either way
The smallest coin value; the minimum amount for קידושין
He cut it off, splitting his statement into separate parts
Counting along: adding up step by step toward one total
Or perhaps: brings in the other side of the question

steps.confusionAlert: The main problem here is that each half came with less than a פרוטה (and if the acts are split, each one also betroths only half a woman). The question is only whether we treat the two halves as separate acts or as one.

phrases.english: Rava asked: "Half of you with half a peruta,
and half of you with half a peruta": what is the law?
Since he said to her "half a peruta," he cut it into separate parts,
or perhaps he is just counting along?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new topic, unrelated to the קדשים lessons before it.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether two half-פרוטה statements count as separate acts (no קידושין) or as one counted-up betrothal (valid).

steps.title: Betrothing each half of a woman with a full coin
steps.stepSummary: If the first case counts as "counting along," רבא asks a harder case: a full פרוטה for each half. Saying a full coin for each half looks even more like two separate betrothals, and you cannot betroth half a woman.
steps.simpleTranslation: If you say he was counting along, then what if he said "Half of you with a פרוטה and half of you with a פרוטה"? Since he gave a full פרוטה each time, did he split his words into two separate betrothals? Or maybe anything done that same day still counts as counting along?
steps.whatsHappening: רבא builds a second question that only comes up if the first one is answered "counting along."
steps.deeperAnalysis: Here each half got a full, valid פרוטה. That makes it look much more like he meant two complete, separate acts. But betrothing only half a woman does not work, so if the acts are separate, nothing happens. The other side says that whatever he does on the same day is still part of one counted-up betrothal.

keyTerms.meaning: If you end up saying: answer the first question this way, then ask the next
He cut off his words into separate statements
Anything done within that same day

steps.whyThisMatters: The "if you say" pattern shows that the second case is harder. Even someone who allows the first case might still say this one is split.

phrases.aramaic: אִם תִּימְצֵי לוֹמַר מוֹנֶה וְהוֹלֵךְ הוּא,
phrases.english: If you end up saying he is counting along,
then "half of you with a peruta and half of you with a peruta": what is the law?
Since he said to her "with a peruta and a peruta,"
he cut his words into separate parts,
or perhaps anything done on that same day
counts as counting along?

steps.triggerLanguage: אִם תִּימְצֵי לוֹמַר מוֹנֶה וְהוֹלֵךְ הוּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Builds on step 2: assuming "counting along" in the half-פרוטה case, it asks about a full פרוטה per half.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether a full פרוטה for each half makes two separate (and therefore failed) half-betrothals, or whether acts on the same day still join into one betrothal.

steps.title: Half today, half tomorrow
steps.stepSummary: Suppose that anything said on the same day counts as 'counting along.' רבא then asks: what if one half is betrothed today and the other half tomorrow?
steps.simpleTranslation: If you say that whatever he says within one day is still 'counting along,' what if he said: 'Half of you with a פרוטה today, and half of you with a פרוטה tomorrow'? Did saying 'tomorrow' cut it into two separate parts? Or does he mean that the קידושין start now and only finish tomorrow?
steps.whatsHappening: רבא climbs one more rung. He takes the lenient answer to the last question and asks whether it still works when the two halves are a day apart.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Until now both halves were given on the same day. Here the word 'tomorrow' adds a time gap. One side says the gap breaks the קידושין into two halves that cannot work. The other side says it is one קידושין that simply takes until tomorrow to be finished.

keyTerms.meaning: If you say (if you end up deciding); the earlier question is assumed to be answered this way
Counting along, building step by step toward one complete act
He cut it off, separating it into two parts
They begin
Now

phrases.english: If you say
that anything within the same day counts as counting along,
"Half of you with a peruta today
and half of you with a peruta tomorrow," what is the law?
Since he said to her "tomorrow," he cut it off,
or perhaps this is what he is saying to her:
"The betrothal begins from now
and will not be completed until tomorrow"?

steps.triggerLanguage: אִם תִּימְצֵי לוֹמַר כֹּל בְּיוֹמֵיהּ מוֹנֶה וְהוֹלֵךְ הוּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Builds on the lenient answer to step 3 and adds a time gap between the two halves.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Does a one-day gap break the קידושין into two separate halves, or is it one קידושין that is completed tomorrow?

steps.title: Your two halves for one coin
steps.stepSummary: רבא asks about 'your two halves with one פרוטה.' This is said all at once, but it still mentions halves. The questions are left unresolved with תיקו.
steps.simpleTranslation: What if he said, 'Your two halves are betrothed with one פרוטה'? Here he certainly said it all at one time. Or perhaps a woman cannot be betrothed in halves at all? It stands unresolved.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא asks a new version of the question in which everything is said together but is still put in terms of 'halves.' The גמרא then ends the whole series of questions with תיקו.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the earlier cases the problem was that the speech was split up. Here there is only one statement and one פרוטה, so that problem is gone. The open question is whether simply describing her as 'two halves' is enough to spoil the קידושין.

keyTerms.meaning: Your two halves
At one time, all at once
In halves
Let it stand; the question stays unresolved

steps.confusionAlert: This תיקו applies to the whole chain of רבא's questions, including the earlier steps. None of them gets an answer.
steps.whatToRemember: All of רבא's 'halves' questions end in תיקו. The basic rule stays in place: a woman cannot be betrothed in halves. It is unclear how far the 'counting along' idea can stretch.

phrases.english: "Your two halves with one peruta," what is the law?

phrases.aramaic: הָכָא וַדַּאי בְּחַד זִימְנָא קָאָמַר לַהּ,
phrases.english: Here he certainly said it to her at one time,

phrases.aramaic: אוֹ דִילְמָא אֵין אִשָּׁה מִתְקַדֶּשֶׁת לַחֲצָאִין כְּלָל?
phrases.english: or perhaps a woman cannot be betrothed in halves at all?
Let it stand.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Takes away the split speech and the split coin, leaving only the word 'halves,' and then closes the series with תיקו.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Is it the split statement that ruins the קידושין, or does any mention of 'halves' ruin it?

steps.title: Two daughters to two sons for one coin
steps.stepSummary: רבא asks whether one פרוטה given by one father to another can betroth two daughters to two sons. The question is left unresolved.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא asked: 'Your two daughters to my two sons with one פרוטה,' what is the law? Do we look at the one giving and the one receiving, and between them there is money? Or do we look at the couples themselves, and for each couple there is not a full פרוטה? It stands unresolved.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא opens a new question. One coin passes between two fathers, but it is meant to create two marriages.
steps.deeperAnalysis: There is one giver and one receiver, so a full פרוטה does change hands. But there are two couples, so each couple gets only half a פרוטה. The question is which of these counts.

keyTerms.meaning: He asks a question (a dilemma)
The giver and the receiver
Money, here meaning a full פרוטה's worth
Their own, meaning the couples being married

phrases.aramaic: בָּעֵי רָבָא: ״שְׁתֵּי בְנוֹתֶיךָ לִשְׁנֵי בָנַי בִּפְרוּטָה״ מַהוּ?
phrases.english: Rava asks: "Your two daughters to my two sons with one peruta," what is the law?

phrases.aramaic: בָּתַר נוֹתֵן וּמְקַבֵּל אָזְלִינַן וְהָאִיכָּא מָמוֹנָא,
phrases.english: Do we go by the giver and receiver, and there is money here,
phrases.notes: The two fathers: one gives a full פרוטה and the other receives it.

phrases.aramaic: אוֹ דִילְמָא בָּתַר דִּידְהוּ אָזְלִינַן וְהָא לֵיכָּא?
phrases.english: or perhaps we go by them themselves, and there is not?
phrases.notes: 'Them' means the sons and daughters. Each couple only gets half a פרוטה.

phrases.english: Let it stand.

steps.triggerLanguage: בָּעֵי רָבָא שְׁתֵּי בְנוֹתֶיךָ לִשְׁנֵי בָנַי בִּפְרוּטָה מַהוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from splitting one woman into halves to splitting one coin across several couples.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Is the minimum of a פרוטה measured by what passes between the giver and the receiver, or by what each couple gets?

steps.title: A daughter and a cow for one coin
steps.stepSummary: רב פפא asks about one פרוטה given for both a daughter and a cow. Is the coin split between them, or does all of it go to the קידושין while the cow is acquired another way? The question is left unresolved.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב פפא asked: 'Your daughter and your cow with one פרוטה,' what is the law? Do we say he meant your daughter with half a פרוטה and your cow with half a פרוטה? Or perhaps he meant your daughter with the פרוטה and your cow by pulling it? It stands unresolved.
steps.whatsHappening: רב פפא asks a related question. One coin is mentioned for two different things: a marriage and a purchase.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the coin is split, each half is less than a פרוטה, so neither the קידושין nor the purchase works. But a cow can also be bought by pulling it (משיכה). So perhaps the whole פרוטה is meant for the daughter, and the cow is acquired by pulling.

keyTerms.meaning: Do we say?
Your cow
Half a פרוטה, less than the minimum
Pulling, a way to acquire an animal

steps.whatToRemember: These questions all ask how one פרוטה is divided when it is meant for more than one thing or person. Each one ends in תיקו.

phrases.aramaic: בָּעֵי רַב פָּפָּא: ״בִּתְּךָ וּפָרָתְךָ בִּפְרוּטָה״ מַהוּ?
phrases.english: Rav Pappa asks: "Your daughter and your cow with one peruta," what is the law?
Do we say: your daughter with half a peruta
and your cow with half a peruta,
or perhaps: your daughter with the peruta
and your cow by pulling?
phrases.notes: Pulling the animal is a way to buy it, so the whole coin can go toward the daughter.

phrases.english: Let it stand.

steps.triggerLanguage: בָּעֵי רַב פָּפָּא בִּתְּךָ וּפָרָתְךָ בִּפְרוּטָה מַהוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Like step 6, it shares one פרוטה between two things, but here one is a marriage and the other is a purchase.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Is the פרוטה split between the daughter and the cow, or does it all go to the קידושין while the cow is acquired by משיכה?

steps.title: One coin for a daughter and land together
steps.stepSummary: רב אשי asks what happens when one פרוטה is given for both a daughter (קידושין) and land. Is the coin split in half, or does the whole coin go to the קידושין while the land is acquired by חזקה? The question is left as תיקו.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אשי asked: if someone says 'your daughter and your land for one פרוטה,' what is the law? Does it mean half a פרוטה for the daughter and half for the land? Or the whole פרוטה for the daughter, with the land acquired by taking possession? It stays unresolved.
steps.whatsHappening: רב אשי asks one more question just like רב פפא's question about the daughter and the cow, but now the second item is land. The question is left unresolved.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Land, unlike a cow, can be acquired by חזקה (doing an owner's act on it), so it does not need the money. That means the whole פרוטה might go to the קידושין, which would make it valid. But if the coin is split, the daughter only gets half a פרוטה, and that is too little for קידושין.

keyTerms.meaning: He asked (a real question, looking for an answer)
Land, real estate
Acquiring land by acting like an owner (fencing, locking, building)
Let it stand; the question stays unresolved

steps.whatToRemember: Every question in this series (steps 2–8) ends in תיקו. רבא's first questions (steps 2–5) ask about betrothing a woman in halves. The later questions (steps 6–8) ask how one פרוטה is divided when it is meant for more than one person or thing.

phrases.english: Rav Ashi asked:
"Your daughter and your land for one perutah": what is the law?
Your daughter with half a perutah
and your land with half a perutah,
or perhaps your daughter with the whole perutah
and your land by taking possession?
Let it stand unresolved.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: The same question as רב פפא's cow case, but with land, which can be acquired by חזקה.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Is one פרוטה given for a daughter and land split between them, or does it all go to the קידושין while the land is acquired by חזקה?

steps.title: Betrothal with silk: is an appraisal needed?
steps.stepSummary: A man was מקדש a woman with silk garments. רבה says no appraisal is needed. רב יוסף says an appraisal is needed.
steps.simpleTranslation: A certain man made קידושין with silk. רבה said: they do not need to be appraised. רב יוסף said: they do need to be appraised.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts a new topic: a real case of קידושין done with silk instead of money. רבה and רב יוסף argue about whether someone must first check what the silk is worth.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Silk is clearly worth more than a פרוטה, so the question is not whether it is enough. The question is whether קידושין done with an object (rather than coins) needs a clear, agreed value first. The next steps narrow down when this argument really applies.

keyTerms.meaning: Silk garments
An appraisal, an estimate of value
They need (it is required)

phrases.english: A certain man betrothed with silk garments,
Rabba said: they do not need an appraisal.
Rav Yosef said: they need an appraisal.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new topic. It moves from 'one פרוטה for several things' to קידושין done with an object instead of money.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רבה: silk used for קידושין does not need appraisal. רב יוסף: it does.

steps.title: Two cases where everyone agrees
steps.stepSummary: If he said 'for any amount,' everyone agrees no appraisal is needed. If he said 'fifty' and the silk is not worth fifty, the קידושין fails because it is not worth what he said.
steps.simpleTranslation: If he told her 'be betrothed with this, whatever it is worth,' everyone agrees no appraisal is needed. If he told her it is worth fifty and it is not worth fifty, then it simply is not worth what he said.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא sets aside two cases where there is no argument at all. This prepares us to see exactly where רבה and רב יוסף do argue.
steps.deeperAnalysis: With 'any amount,' she accepted the silk whatever its value, so its value does not matter. With a false 'fifty,' she was misled, so the קידושין does not work. That leaves only one case open: he said fifty and it really is worth fifty.

keyTerms.meaning: For any amount at all, whatever it is worth
Everyone (both sides agree)
Fifty

phrases.english: If he said to her: with any amount,
everyone agrees
that they do not need an appraisal.
If he said to her: "fifty,"
phrases.notes: He means the silk is worth fifty דינר. The coin name is left out but understood.

phrases.english: and they are not worth fifty,
then they are just not worth it.
phrases.notes: In other words, the קידושין fails because he promised something that is not true.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Narrows the dispute from step 9 by removing the cases where both agree.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: 'Any amount': no appraisal needed, by everyone. A false 'fifty': it does not work, by everyone.

steps.title: The real dispute and each side's reason
steps.stepSummary: They argue when he said 'fifty' and it really is worth fifty. רבה: no appraisal needed, since it is worth fifty. רב יוסף: an appraisal is needed, because a woman who cannot judge value does not truly rely on his word.
steps.simpleTranslation: The argument is when he said fifty and it is really worth fifty. רבה says no appraisal is needed, because it is worth fifty. רב יוסף says an appraisal is needed: since the woman is not an expert in values, she does not feel sure, so she does not fully agree.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pinpoints the exact case of the argument and gives each side's reason.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבה looks at the facts: the silk really is worth fifty, so the deal is good. רב יוסף looks at the woman's mind: she could not know it was worth fifty, so she never firmly agreed. Without her firm agreement, the קידושין does not take effect.

keyTerms.meaning: Where they do argue
Expert, knowledgeable (said of a woman)
Her mind relies; she feels sure and truly agrees

steps.whatToRemember: In the main version, the argument is only when he said 'fifty' and it really is worth fifty. רבה looks at the real value, and רב יוסף looks at whether she felt sure.
steps.confusionAlert: רב יוסף is not saying the silk is worth too little. It really is worth fifty. His problem is that she could not know that, so her agreement was not firm.

phrases.english: Where they disagree is when he said "fifty"
and they are worth fifty.
Rabba said: they do not need an appraisal,
since they are worth fifty.
Rav Yosef said: they need an appraisal,
since a woman is not expert in appraising,
she does not feel sure (and so does not fully agree).

steps.triggerLanguage: כִּי פְּלִיגִי, דְּאָמַר חַמְשִׁין וְשָׁווּ חַמְשִׁין
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the agreed cases are removed, this gives the one case where they argue and each side's reason.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: When he said 'fifty' and it is worth fifty: רבה says no appraisal is needed; רב יוסף says it is needed, because she does not feel sure.

steps.title: Second version: they argue even over 'any amount'
steps.stepSummary: Another version says רבה and רב יוסף argue even when he said 'for any amount.' It begins רב יוסף's reason: שוה כסף is like כסף, and just as money has a fixed value… (the sentence continues in the next section).
steps.simpleTranslation: Some say they argue even when he said 'whatever it is worth.' רב יוסף said: something worth money is like money. Just as money has a set value…
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a second version (איכא דאמרי) that makes the argument wider. It starts explaining רב יוסף's reason, which finishes in the next section.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the first version, everyone agreed that 'any amount' needs no appraisal. Here, רב יוסף requires an appraisal even then. His reason is a comparison: an object used as payment (שוה כסף) must work like coins, and coins have a known, fixed value.

keyTerms.meaning: There are those who say (a second version of the discussion)
Something worth money (an object used in place of coins)
Fixed, with a set value

steps.confusionAlert: This sentence is not finished here. The comparison 'just as money is fixed…' is completed in the next section.

phrases.english: There are those who say
they disagree even when he said "any amount."

phrases.aramaic: רַב יוֹסֵף אָמַר: שָׁוֶה כֶּסֶף הֲרֵי הוּא כְּכֶסֶף,
phrases.english: Rav Yosef said: something worth money is like money,
just as money is fixed (has a set value)…

steps.triggerLanguage: אִיכָּא דְּאָמְרִי בְּכֹל דְּהוּ נָמֵי פְּלִיגִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a different version of the dispute, saying they argue even in the 'any amount' case that step 10 treated as agreed.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: In this version, רב יוסף requires an appraisal even for 'any amount,' because שוה כסף must be like כסף, which has a fixed value.
